description: Effect priors from randomized / long-term controlled trials and meta-analyses relevant to central Iowa corn-soy, plus observational contrasts and context records (use_as_prior=false), citation checks and shock years. Effects are % change of treatment vs control unless the unit says otherwise; negative = reduction. For E5 the treatment is the corn-soy rotation and the control is continuous corn (benefit as % of CC yield). Only priors with prior_kind='numeric' have a usable effect.mean; 'counts', 'range' and 'qualitative' records have mean=null and use_as_prior=false. Strategy IDs E1..E5 are evidence IDs, NOT web card IDs: join to web/data/effects.json via web_strategy_id (or web_strategy_map), never on strategy_id. web_unit_compatible=false means the value must be converted as described in `conversion` before it can fill the web_key outcome.

effect.unit: % change maize yield, no-till vs conventional tillage

uncertainty.note: all-conditions maize value; maize in humid climates did not recover to CT yields after 3-10 yr

priors.source: Pittelkow C.M. et al. (2015) When does no-till yield more? A global meta-analysis. Field Crops Research 183:156-168
priors.summary: No-till cut maize yields about 7.6% on average, and humid-climate maize did not catch up over time.
priors.applicability: Central Iowa is humid, so a maize penalty is plausible. Overall no-till penalty is -4% with N fertilizer and -12% without. Companion Nature paper (Pittelkow et al. 2015, Nature 517:365-368, doi:10.1038/nature13809; 5463 obs, 610 studies) says no-till reduces yields on average, with smaller losses when combined with residue retention and rotation. A '5.7%' overall figure could not be confirmed.

priors.summary: Moldboard plowing can strip up to ~30 t/ha/yr off convex knolls; no-till sets this term near zero.

priors.conversion: absolute: t/ha/yr x 0.4461 = short t/ac/yr (30 t/ha/yr = 13.4 short t/ac/yr upper value on convex knolls)

citation_checks.claim: PCCP 2021 enrolled '12.2 million acres' (design doc: '12.2M acres vs 5M forecast')
citation_checks.corrected_statement: About 12.2 million net acres received the $5/acre premium reduction under the 2021 Pandemic Cover Crop Program (FCIC/RMA final rule establishing the 2022 PCCP). American Farmland Trust's analysis of RMA Summary of Business data gives a total 2021 cost of $59.4 million. No source was found for a '5 million acre forecast'; drop that comparison or cite it separately.
citation_checks.evidence: Rule text, Cost Benefit Analysis Summary: 'Approximately 12.2 million net acres have received a premium reduction for the crop year 2021 PCCP'. The same rule projects 23 million eligible acres and $116.2M for 2022.

citation_checks.claim: Kluger, Di Tommaso & Lobell 2025 'Precrop Payoffs': journal/volume/article id; 'median precrop benefit 4.5%'
citation_checks.corrected_statement: Kluger D.M., Di Tommaso S., Lobell D.B. (2025). Precrop payoffs: causal machine learning reveals large but variable yield benefits of crop rotation in major breadbaskets. Environmental Research Letters 20(11): 114037 (published online 17 Oct 2025). doi:10.1088/1748-9326/ae0f45. The paper reports a median estimated NET rotation benefit of 4.5% on yield across all 36 precrop x outcome-crop x country combinations (US, Canada, France, China). It is not a US corn-soy figure: US soybean->corn = +2.5%, US corn->soybean = +8.5% (Table S9).
citation_checks.evidence: Crossref metadata (volume 20, issue 11, article 114037). The 4.5% median sentence appears in the Discussion of arXiv v2 (Oct 2025), which corresponds to the accepted version.

citation_checks.claim: Won et al. 2024 AJAE: '$40M per 1 percent' cover crop adoption reduction in prevented-planting losses
citation_checks.corrected_statement: Won S., Rejesus R.M., Goodwin B.K., Aglasan S. (2024) Am. J. Agric. Econ. 106(2):659-683 (online Feb 2023), doi:10.1111/ajae.12396. Using 2019 values, a ONE-PERCENTAGE-POINT increase in cover crop adoption (~3.9 million acres nationally) is estimated to lower the prevented-planting loss ratio from 4.47% to 4.43%. With $96.73B liabilities, that is about $38.69 million less in prevented-planting indemnities for 2019. 'Nearly $40 million per 1%' is press-release wording (NC State). It is a percentage-point change and a one-year (2019) counterfactual, not an annual recurring saving.
citation_checks.evidence: Publisher full text was blocked (HTTP 403) from this environment. The percentage-point wording and the $38.69M / 4.47->4.43% / 3.9M-acre figures come from a search-engine extraction of the Wiley article page. The press release says '1% increase ... nearly $40 million'.
citation_checks.verification: secondary (re-check the paper's Section on economic significance before printing)

shock_years.method: Drought classification from USDM weekly county statistics for Story, Boone, Polk, Marshall, Hamilton, Hardin, Jasper, Dallas (pipeline/evidence_usdm.py). Growing season = May-Sep. D1+ = moderate drought or worse.

source.name: US Drought Monitor county statistics (categorical cumulative % area; 8 core tile counties averaged)

events.detail: Derecho crossed central Iowa late morning to early afternoon of 10 Aug 2020 (a seismometer near Des Moines recorded the winds ~10:26-12:08 local). The official peak in the NWS Des Moines area was 99 mph at Marshalltown ASOS. Storm reports came from Story (Ames, Nevada), Polk, Marshall, Boone, Jasper, Dallas, Hardin and Tama counties, with flattened corn and defoliated soybeans. NOAA NCEI lists the event at $11.0B (Historic Midwest Derecho). Drought (USDM D1+) also developed Jul-Oct 2020: core-county D1+ 79% Aug, 95% Sep; D2+ 46-52%.

sources.name: NWS Des Moines, August 10, 2020 Derecho event page
US Drought Monitor county statistics (categorical cumulative % area; 8 core tile counties averaged)

events.detail: Strongest in-season drought of 2016-2024 in the tile counties: D1+ 93-97% of area Jun-Sep, D2+ 48-59% Jun-Aug, D3 ~14% in Aug. Not in the design's hindcast window, but must be flagged as a drought year (Iowa still posted high yields in 2021, so drought != yield loss).

sources.name: US Drought Monitor county statistics (categorical cumulative % area; 8 core tile counties averaged)

events.detail: May-Jul 2022 had essentially no drought in the core counties (D1+ 0%). Drought developed in August (D1+ 38%, D2+ 6%), eased in September (D1+ 27%) and intensified in Oct-Dec (D1+ 73-100%). Iowa DNR water summaries describe drought worsening from late summer into fall, especially in central and east-central Iowa. Impact on 2022 grain fill is real but late; treat as a moderate, late-season shock.

sources.name: US Drought Monitor county statistics (categorical cumulative % area; 8 core tile counties averaged)
Iowa DNR Water Summary Update, Oct 2022

events.type: growing-season dryness escalating to drought late summer
events.detail: Core counties were abnormally dry (D0) over ~100% of area Jun-Sep. D1+ was 13% (Jun), 29% (Jul), 34% (Aug), then 97% in Sep with D2+ 49%. NWS Des Moines reported much of central and west-central Iowa in D2 by September, with D3 expanding into central Iowa by December 2023.

sources.name: US Drought Monitor county statistics (categorical cumulative % area; 8 core tile counties averaged)
NWS Des Moines Drought Information Statement, 28 Sep 2023
NWS Des Moines Drought Information Statement, 21 Dec 2023

shock_years.assessment_for_hindcast: The region.json hindcast event ('2022-2023 Midwest drought') is supported, with a caveat. In the tile counties, 2022 drought began in August and 2023 drought (D1+) covered only 13-34% of the area until September. By USDM, 2021 was the most severe in-season drought year in the 2016-2024 panel and sits inside the training window (2016-2021). Phase 2 should define drought_flag from weather data (POWER/IMERG precipitation and heat, or these USDM values) instead of assuming whole-season drought in 2022-2023, and should either treat 2021 as a drought year in training or note it explicitly.
